parts.title: Part 1
parts.context: A father phones about a summer camp for his son.
script: A
Hello, Lakeside Summer Camps, Jenny speaking.
B
Hi. I'd like to book a place on one of your camps for my son.
A
Lovely. Can I take your surname?
B
Mahmud. M, A, H, M, U, D.
A
Thank you. And how old is your son?
B
He's thirteen. He'll be fourteen in September.
A
So he can join the camps for twelve to fifteen-year-olds. We have two this summer: a science camp and an adventure camp.
B
He enjoys science, but he really wants to be outdoors, so the adventure camp, please.
A
Good choice. That runs for one week, starting on the fourth of August.
B
What sort of activities are there?
A
Kayaking on the lake, hiking, and climbing on our outdoor wall. All with qualified instructors, of course.
B
And where do the children sleep?
A
They used to sleep in tents, but this year we've built new wooden cabins, with six children in each.
B
That sounds much more comfortable. How much does it cost?
A
The adventure camp is four hundred and eighty pounds, including all meals and equipment.
B
Is there any discount? His sister might come next year.
A
Yes, if you book a second child at the same time, you get ten percent off the second place.
B
Good to know. Oh, and he has an allergy. He can't eat nuts.
A
Thank you for telling us. I'll make a note, and our kitchen is very careful about that.
B
Is there anything he needs to bring?
A
We provide all the equipment, but he'll need to bring his own sleeping bag.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: A council officer explains changes to household rubbish collection.
script: A
Good evening. I'm David Grant from the town council, and I'm here to explain the changes to rubbish and recycling collections.
A
Why are we changing the system? Some of you have assumed it's to save money, but the main reason is that new national rules require all councils to collect food waste separately.
A
The new system will start on the first of April. We'd hoped to start in March, but the new bins took longer to arrive than expected.
A

Recycling will be collected every week, and general waste, the black bin, will now be collected every two weeks instead of weekly. Because more of your rubbish will go into recycling, we don't expect this to be a problem.
A
You don't need to order anything. New bins will be delivered to every household during March.
A
So what goes where? The blue bin is for paper and cardboard, such as newspapers and cereal boxes. However, pizza boxes covered in grease can't be recycled, so they should go in general waste.
A

The green bin is for plastic bottles, cans and glass jars. Please rinse them first. Plastic bags are not accepted in any recycling bin, as they damage the sorting machines, so put them in general waste or take them back to supermarkets.
A
Finally, the brown bin is for food waste, like vegetable peelings and leftovers, and also for garden waste, such as grass cuttings and leaves.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: Two business students, Aisha and Marcus, plan a social media strategy for a café.
script: A
So, Aisha, we need to plan the social media strategy for the café for our marketing assignment.
B
Right. When we interviewed the owner, I thought she'd say she wanted more weekend customers, but her main goal is to attract more students during the week.
A
That makes sense, with the university so close. What did our survey show about how students find new cafés?
B
Mostly through recommendations from friends. Online reviews came second.
A
Interesting. I think we should do lots of short videos.
B
Videos work well, but my worry is that they take a lot of time to produce, and the owner is very busy.
A
True. What about a budget for paid advertising?
B
I'd suggest a small amount for paid ads aimed at students, rather than nothing at all. Without any paid promotion, it's hard to reach new people.
A
OK. And how will we measure whether it's working?
B
We could give a discount code in the posts and count how many people use it in the café.
A
Good. Now, which channel for which purpose? I think the video app is ideal for showing behind-the-scenes baking.
B
Agreed. Special offers for regular customers should go in the email newsletter, since they've already signed up.
A
And pictures of new menu items work best on the photo app.
B
Customers' own photos and reviews too. People like seeing those on the photo app.
A
And the monthly calendar of events, like quiz nights?
B
That's best in the newsletter, so people can keep it for reference.

parts.title: Part 4
script: A
Good morning. Today's lecture is about one of the most important weather systems on Earth: the monsoon.
A
The word monsoon comes from an Arabic word meaning season. A monsoon is a seasonal change in the direction of the prevailing winds, which brings a dramatic change in rainfall.
A

The basic cause is the difference in temperature between land and sea. In summer, land heats up much faster than the sea. Warm air rises over the land, and moist air from the ocean flows in to replace it, bringing heavy rain.
A
In South Asia, the summer monsoon brings around eighty percent of the region's annual rainfall in just four months. Hundreds of millions of farmers depend on it to grow crops such as rice.
A

The amounts of rain can be extraordinary. Cherrapunji, in north-east India, close to the border with Bangladesh, is one of the wettest places on Earth, receiving more than eleven metres of rain in an average year.
A

Because so much depends on the monsoon, any change in its timing is serious. If the rains arrive late or are weaker than usual, the result can be drought and crop failure. If they're too heavy, they cause floods and landslides.
A
Climate change appears to be making the monsoon more extreme. Studies suggest that there are now fewer days of moderate rain and more days of very heavy rain, with longer dry periods in between.
A

Forecasting has improved greatly, thanks largely to data from satellites. And in countries like Bangladesh, early warning systems now send text messages to millions of people when floods are expected, which has helped to reduce the number of deaths.

passages.title: The Remarkable Octopus
paragraphs: Few animals seem as alien as the octopus. It has three hearts, two of which pump blood through the gills while the third serves the rest of the body. Its blood is blue, because it uses a copper-based molecule rather than iron to carry oxygen. And it has around 500 million neurons, a number comparable to that of a dog, but organised very differently: about two-thirds of them are found not in the brain but in the eight arms.

This unusual nervous system means that each arm can, to some extent, act independently. An arm that has been separated from the body can still reach for food and pass it towards where the mouth would be. Scientists believe that the brain sets general goals while the arms work out many of the details themselves.

Octopuses are masters of disguise. Their skin contains thousands of cells called chromatophores, filled with pigment, which can be expanded or contracted in a fraction of a second to change colour and pattern. Some species can also change the texture of their skin to resemble rock or seaweed. Remarkably, most species are thought to be colour-blind, and scientists are still investigating how they manage to match their surroundings so accurately.

Octopuses also show signs of intelligence that surprise many researchers. In 2009, scientists in Indonesia filmed veined octopuses collecting coconut shells from the sea floor, carrying them across the seabed and later assembling them into shelters, one of the first recorded examples of tool use by an invertebrate. In captivity, octopuses have learned to open jars, recognise individual people and escape from their tanks. In 2016, an octopus named Inky escaped from his tank at the National Aquarium of New Zealand, crossed the floor and slipped down a drain pipe that led to the sea.

What makes this intelligence puzzling is how short the animals' lives are. Most octopuses live for only one or two years. Females lay a single batch of eggs, guard them without eating, and usually die soon after the eggs hatch. Intelligence is usually associated with long-lived social animals, such as apes and dolphins, that learn from others over many years.

Some scientists suggest that octopus intelligence evolved after their ancestors lost the protective shell that their relatives, such as the nautilus, still have. Without a shell, they became vulnerable to predators, and survival may have depended on the ability to hide, escape and find food in flexible ways. Whatever the explanation, the octopus shows that complex minds can evolve along very different paths from our own.

passages.title: The Bicycle
paragraphs: The first ancestor of the bicycle had no pedals at all. In 1817 the German inventor Karl Drais demonstrated his 'running machine', a wooden frame with two wheels on which the rider sat and pushed along the ground with his feet. One theory suggests that Drais was inspired by a shortage of horses, many of which had died or been slaughtered after the crop failures of 1816, a year so cold that it became known as 'the year without a summer'.

In the 1860s, French makers attached pedals directly to the front wheel, creating the velocipede. These machines were heavy, with iron-rimmed wooden wheels, and on the poor roads of the time they gave such an uncomfortable ride that they became known as 'boneshakers'. Nevertheless, they created a short-lived craze, with riding schools opening in Paris, London and New York.

Because the pedals turned the front wheel directly, a larger wheel meant that the rider travelled further with each turn of the pedals. Makers therefore built front wheels of ever greater size, leading to the penny-farthing of the 1870s, with a front wheel up to one and a half metres high and a tiny rear one. The penny-farthing was fast but dangerous: riders sat high above the ground and were often thrown forward over the handlebars when the wheel hit a stone.

The design that changed everything appeared in 1885. John Kemp Starley's Rover 'safety bicycle' had two wheels of similar size, with the rear wheel driven by a chain. This allowed speed without a giant wheel, and riders could put their feet on the ground. Three years later, John Boyd Dunlop developed the pneumatic tyre, originally to make his young son's tricycle more comfortable. With air-filled tyres, the safety bicycle became smooth, practical and enormously popular. Its basic shape has hardly changed since.

The bicycle's social impact was profound. For the first time, ordinary people could travel independently and cheaply beyond their own neighbourhoods. The effect on women was especially significant. Cycling encouraged more practical clothing and gave women a new freedom of movement, and some campaigners for women's rights argued that the bicycle had done more for women's independence than almost anything else.

After decades in which cars dominated many cities, the bicycle is enjoying a revival. Bike-sharing schemes operate in hundreds of cities, electric bikes have made cycling possible for people who live in hilly areas or travel long distances, and many cities are building protected cycle lanes. In the Netherlands, there are now more bicycles than people.

passages.title: A Gentle Push
paragraphs: In 2008 the economist Richard Thaler and the legal scholar Cass Sunstein published a book called Nudge, which quickly became one of the most influential works of public policy of the century. Its central idea was that people's decisions are strongly influenced by the way choices are presented to them, which the authors called 'choice architecture'. By designing that architecture carefully, governments and organisations could 'nudge' people towards better decisions without forcing them or removing any options.

The most striking evidence concerns default options, the choice that applies if a person does nothing. In countries where citizens are automatically registered as organ donors unless they opt out, registration rates are typically far higher than in countries where people must actively opt in. Similarly, when companies automatically enrol employees in pension schemes, while allowing them to leave, participation rises dramatically.

Other nudges rely on social norms. In 2010 the British government set up the Behavioural Insights Team, often called the 'Nudge Unit', to apply these ideas to policy. In one of its best-known trials, letters to people who had not paid their taxes were changed to include a single sentence stating that most people in their town had already paid on time. Payment rates increased significantly. A more playful example is the image of a fly printed inside urinals at Amsterdam's Schiphol Airport, which gives men something to aim at and is said to have greatly reduced cleaning costs.

Thaler and Sunstein describe their approach as 'libertarian paternalism': it steers people in a particular direction while preserving their freedom of choice. Critics, however, argue that nudging can be a form of manipulation, since it works by exploiting psychological tendencies of which people are often unaware. They also ask who decides what counts as a 'better' choice.

More recently, doubts have grown about how powerful nudges really are. Early studies often reported large effects, but studies with positive results are more likely to be published than those that find nothing. A 2022 analysis that attempted to correct for this bias concluded that the evidence for many types of nudge was much weaker than had been thought. In my view, this does not mean that nudges are useless; default options in particular appear to have real and lasting effects. But it does suggest that their benefits have sometimes been exaggerated.

The danger is that governments may see nudges as a cheap and politically easy alternative to more difficult measures. A sign encouraging people to take the stairs is unlikely to solve obesity, and a reminder to save energy will not stop climate change. I believe nudges are a useful addition to the policy toolkit, but serious problems require stronger measures, such as regulation and taxation, which nudges should support rather than replace.

task1.text: The table below shows average house prices, in thousands of US dollars, in five cities in 2015 and 2025. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.
model: The table compares average house prices in Sydney, London, Toronto, Dublin and Tokyo in 2015 and 2025.

Overall, prices rose in all five cities over the decade, but the size of the increase varied considerably. Sydney remained the most expensive city throughout, while Toronto and Dublin saw the fastest growth.
In 2015, an average house in Sydney cost $800,000, followed by London at $650,000 and Toronto at $550,000. Tokyo and Dublin were the least expensive, at $450,000 and $300,000 respectively.

By 2025, the average price in Sydney had risen by $350,000 to $1.15 million. Toronto experienced an even larger relative increase, of more than 60%, to $900,000, which meant that it overtook London. Dublin's prices also rose by 60%, to $480,000. By contrast, growth in London and Tokyo was modest, with prices increasing to $720,000 and $520,000 respectively.

task2.text: Some people believe that advertising aimed at children should be banned. To what extent do you agree or disagree? Write at least 250 words.
model: Children today are exposed to large amounts of advertising, not only on television but also in apps, games and online videos. I largely agree that advertising aimed at children should be banned, because young children cannot understand or resist persuasive messages in the way adults can.

The main argument for a ban is that children are especially vulnerable. Research suggests that young children often cannot distinguish between advertisements and normal programmes, and they generally do not understand that adverts are designed to sell them something. This makes them easy targets. Much of the advertising aimed at children promotes unhealthy food, sugary drinks and expensive toys, which can contribute to obesity and create conflict within families when parents refuse to buy what their children demand.

Opponents of a ban argue that it would harm businesses and reduce funding for children's television, which partly depends on advertising income. They also claim that parents, not governments, should be responsible for what their children watch, and that learning to deal with advertising is part of growing up.

These points have some validity, but I do not find them convincing. Parents cannot monitor every screen their children use, particularly online, where advertising is often disguised as entertainment. Moreover, several countries, such as Sweden and Norway, have restricted advertising to young children for many years without serious damage to their media industries.

In conclusion, although a complete ban may be difficult to enforce online, I believe governments should prohibit advertising aimed at young children, and strictly limit advertising of unhealthy products to older children.

speaking.cue:
Describe a festival or celebration that is important in your country.
You should say:
- what it is
- when it takes place
- what people do
and explain why it is important.
speaking.cueModel: I'd like to talk about Pohela Boishakh, which is the Bengali New Year. It's celebrated on the fourteenth of April, and it's probably the most colourful day of the year in Bangladesh. What makes it special is that it isn't connected to any religion, so everyone celebrates it together. The day usually starts very early. In Dhaka, thousands of people gather in Ramna Park at sunrise to listen to traditional songs. Later in the morning, there's a huge procession organised by students from the Fine Arts faculty, with giant colourful masks and models of animals and birds. People wear traditional clothes, women usually in white saris with red borders, and men in panjabis, and many people paint designs on their faces. Food is a big part of it too. The traditional breakfast is panta bhat, which is rice soaked in water, served with fried hilsa fish. For me, the festival is important because it celebrates our culture and language, rather than any particular group. It's a day when the whole country feels united, and I always feel very proud to be Bangladeshi.
